title: Resolve to Read Complex Stories More Often
author: Admired Leadership
summary: A New Year's piece that argues for sustained reading as a leadership capability rather than a personal enrichment habit. The claim is that screen time has displaced the reading of books and complex material to the point where, for many, it has vanished entirely, and that the cost is the capacity for deep focus itself. The essay's most useful move is to name a self-reinforcing spiral: as leaders shift from books to screens their reading skill atrophies, which makes complex material less rewarding to tackle, which makes them read still less. It treats extended reading as unusual among mental activities because it allows a single topic to sit and marinate, something fragmented phone-supplied information cannot do. Fiction is defended on separate grounds, as empathy practice through inhabiting how other people see things. The resolution offered is directional rather than quantified, more reading and less scanning with each passing year, closed with Fran Lebowitz on reading before thinking.
points: The central argument is that deep reading is not an enrichment activity but the mechanism by which the capacity for sustained attention is maintained, so its loss degrades a leader's core equipment.
The piece names a self-reinforcing spiral worth watching for: less reading produces weaker reading skill, which makes complex material less rewarding, which produces still less reading.
Extended reading is singled out as unlike any other mental activity because it lets one topic sit and marinate, which fragmented phone-supplied information structurally cannot do.
Fiction earns a separate defence on empathy grounds, as practice at imagining how other people and characters experience things.
The prescription is directional rather than a target, more reading and less scanning each year, which sidesteps the usual failure mode of book-count resolutions.
quotes: Time that was once spent reading books and other complex information has dried up, constituting minutes for some and no time at all for others.
We are losing the ability to focus deeply and maintain the resolute attention required for learning.
For many leaders, reading a book or sophisticated monograph is the deepest form of mindful focus they experience.
The capacity for thinking deeply and absorbing real understanding is enhanced by reading texts that can’t be quickly skimmed or scanned.
When leaders consistently expose themselves to the fragmented and disconnected information supplied on their phones, they lose the sense of deep connectedness essential to achieve new insights.
Even reading fiction increases a leader’s empathy, as they get to imagine how other people and characters see and experience things.
